a-crash-course-in-asynchronous-python-12.summary: Explains Python synchronous and asynchronous functions, using asyncio for I/O concurrency and threads or process pools for CPU parallelism.

sections.(intro): This section contains no substantive article text.
sections.How (and when) to undertake task paralle: Introduces asynchronous Python, cautions against copying async patterns without understanding concurrency, and links to code examples.
sections.1\\. The difference between a “normal” a: Defines synchronous functions as thread-blocking, preventing other tasks from starting until they finish.
Uses restaurant ordering to illustrate how asynchronous tasks can wait while other work proceeds.
sections.Back to code: Compares sequential document processing with async functions, showing that awaiting each task sequentially still takes the same time.
sections.2\\. So why don’t we make every function: Introduces reasons asynchronous functions are not always preferable.
sections.Synchronous functions have tracebacks th: Compares straightforward synchronous error tracebacks with more complex async tracebacks caused by tasks resuming at different times.
sections.Async functions have coding overhead: Explains async code's mental overhead and shows that calling a coroutine without awaiting it does not execute it.
sections.3\\. By the way, concurrency does not me: Distinguishes concurrency from parallelism and demonstrates using Python threads to run document-processing tasks concurrently.
sections.Introducing race conditions: Shows how concurrent threads can race when printing and uses a lock to protect output, noting asyncio also provides locks.
sections.Why does threading take the same time as: Explains that Python threads can make concurrent progress but do not necessarily execute tasks in parallel.
sections.Why no true parallelism in Python thread: Describes how the GIL limits Python bytecode execution across threads and recommends asyncio for I/O or threads for synchronous libraries.
sections.4\\. But Python is still able to achieve: Distinguishes I/O-bound concurrency from CPU-bound parallelism and introduces thread and process executors for comparing workloads.
sections.🔹results = list(executor.map(cpu\\_inten: Explains executor.map results and how process pools use separate interpreters and CPU cores for parallel execution.
sections.a. ThreadPoolExecutor with limited worke: Shows how a thread pool with five workers runs ten one-second tasks in two batches.
sections.b. ThreadPoolExecutor with more workers: Shows how twenty thread workers can run ten one-second waiting tasks concurrently in about one second.
sections.c. Asyncio: Explains how an event loop suspends and resumes waiting tasks, allowing ten one-second sleeps to overlap.
sections.d. Process Pool (separate kitchens, sepa: Describes process pools as independent interpreters enabling parallel CPU work, with serialization overhead and little benefit for I/O waits.
sections.Wrapping up: Summarizes that concurrency helps I/O tasks, while separate processes enable CPU-bound parallelism despite the GIL.
sections.Learning by analogies: Recaps analogies distinguishing asynchronous execution, concurrency, and parallelism, and recommends concurrency for I/O and parallelism for CPU work.

a-field-guide-to-multi-agent-architectur.summary: The article explains five multi-agent architectures—hierarchical, workflow, swarm, blackboard, and actor-critic—and compares their coordination mechanisms and use cases with LangChain and LangGraph examples.

sections.(intro): This section contains only a divider and no technical content.
sections.Five Architectures. Five Different Answe: Introduces five multi-agent coordination architectures and frames their differences around how agents coordinate, share information, and control execution.
sections.1\\. Hierarchical Multi-Agent Systems: Explains hierarchical systems in which a supervisor delegates tasks to specialist agents that may have their own tools and sub-agents.
sections.When should you use a hierarchical archi: Describes when hierarchical delegation is useful and discusses supervisor bottlenecks, routing failures, and current LangGraph recommendations.
sections.2\\. Explicit Multi Agent Workflows: Shows how to define multi-agent control flow explicitly, including planning tasks and dispatching specialist work concurrently.
sections.When to use explicit multi agent workflo: Identifies auditability and nonstandard control flow as reasons to use explicit workflows, while noting their implementation burden.
sections.3\\. Agent Swarm: Explains decentralized swarms, where active agents use handoff tools to transfer conversations directly to other specialists.
sections.When should you use a swarm?: Discusses swarms for unpredictable execution paths and their costs in latency, token use, debugging, and observability.
sections.4\\. Blackboard Multi Agent Systems: Introduces blackboard coordination, where specialists contribute to a shared workspace and the evolving solution guides next actions.
sections.a. The blackboard: Defines the blackboard as structured shared problem state with specialist-owned panels, rather than a shared conversation log.
sections.b. Knowledge sources: Describes knowledge sources through their activation conditions and actions, with coordination occurring through the blackboard.
sections.c. The control component: Explains how a controller selects eligible knowledge sources based on current board state and repeats after each contribution.
sections.Execution is deliberately sequential: Explains why blackboard systems activate specialists sequentially, since each contribution can change which action is useful next.
sections.When should you use a blackboard archite: Covers blackboard use cases, modularity, historical applications, and complexity from schemas, activation rules, priorities, and sequential execution.
sections.5\\. Actor-Critic (Adversarial) Multi Ag: Introduces iterative adversarial review with an actor, critic, and judge, separating defect detection from decisions to revise.
sections.a. The Actor: Describes how an actor creates an initial draft and revises it using critique and the judge’s priorities.
sections.b. The critic: Explains structured adversarial critique and severity-weighted issue scores as signals for tracking draft improvement.
sections.c. The judge: Describes how a judge evaluates critique findings and decides whether material problems warrant another revision.
sections.Why a watchdog is still necessary: Explains deterministic round caps and stalemate detection for bounding adversarial review loops that LLM roles cannot reliably terminate.
sections.Finalisation must distinguish success fr: Distinguishes accepted drafts from runs halted by limits or stagnation, which should report unresolved issues.
sections.When should you use an adversarial archi: Discusses iterative review use cases, added model-call costs, overcorrection, inconsistent judgments, and the need for bounded convergence.
sections.Choosing an architecture: Compares the five architectures by identifying who controls the next action in each coordination pattern.
sections.Final Thoughts: Places these architectures in historical context and explains that LLMs provide new reasoning agents for established organizational patterns.

sections.Chat applications: Chat-based coding tools generate code through conversation, typically requiring users to transfer suggested code into their projects.
sections.IDE copilots: IDE copilots suggest and apply code changes within an editor, usually with explicit user approval.
sections.CLI agents: CLI agents inspect and modify codebases, run tests, and iterate; their performance depends on the orchestration harness and setup.

sections.Tip #1: Keep the main agent’s context cl: Delegate specialized tasks to isolated sub-agents so the main agent can orchestrate without accumulating implementation context.
sections.Tip #2: Treat skills as deferred context: Load skill instructions progressively when relevant to avoid context bloat, improve precision, and reduce conflicts.
sections.Tip #3: CLAUDE.md is a control surface,: Use CLAUDE.md for concise project context, architectural conventions, and behavioral constraints that guide the agent.
sections.Tip #4: Use permissions as intentional f: Calibrate agent permissions to balance iteration speed with control over unsafe or unintended changes.
sections.Tip #5: Don’t rebuild what already exist: Use existing plugins, MCP servers, and tools when they provide capabilities that would otherwise require custom implementation.

sections.b. The multi-agent setup: The project uses markdown-defined sub-agents with specialized responsibilities, including a code reviewer with specified tools and review criteria.
sections.c. Generating the prd.md: Claude interviews the author to generate structured project tasks and supporting status and completion files through a custom command.
sections.d. The Ralph Wiggum Agent Loop: The Ralph Wiggum plugin repeatedly runs tasks in fresh agent sessions, validating each task while limiting iterations.
sections.Firing the starting gun 💥: The author starts the workflow by generating requirements and running a Ralph Loop command with sub-agent steps and a completion promise.
sections.Bonus: Here’s how to work with Claude Co: The remote-control command lets users approve requests and send follow-up instructions from a phone while Claude Code runs.
sections.Testing it: The author reports test coverage and explains how to configure Claude Desktop to launch the local MCP service in stdio mode.
sections.Feels like magic doesn’t it? 🪄: The author describes planning, reviewing, and testing AI-generated code, including using CodeRabbit as a second reviewer and tuning its findings.
sections.In closing: The author argues that AI-assisted software development shifts engineering effort from typing code toward architecture, review, orchestration, and judgment.

understanding-blockchains-from-scratch-f.summary: Builds a toy Python blockchain with SHA-256 hash chaining and proof-of-work mining to show how tampering is detected and competing transaction histories are resolved.

sections.(intro): This section contains only a visual divider and no technical discussion.
sections.Building a tiny blockchain from first pr: The article introduces a toy blockchain built in Python to explain hash chaining, tamper detection, and proof-of-work.
sections.First, the high level understanding: Blocks record data and link to earlier blocks, while consensus rules determine valid blocks and accepted history.
sections.The double spend problem: Blockchains let mutually distrustful participants agree on transaction history and prevent double spending without a central referee.
sections.Concept 1: Hash chaining makes history t: Cryptographic hash properties let blocks fingerprint their contents and link to previous blocks, making edits detectable.
sections.Attempt 1: The sloppy attacker: Changing block data without updating its stored hash causes the chain’s integrity check to fail.
sections.Attempt 2: The clever attacker: Recomputing a tampered block’s hash breaks the next block’s reference to its predecessor.
sections.Attempt 3: The actually clever attacker: Rebuilding every descendant hash can restore a tampered chain, motivating a mechanism that makes rewriting costly.
sections.Concept 2: Proof of work — hard to produ: Proof-of-work miners vary a nonce to find a hash meeting a target, while others can verify the result cheaply.
sections.What does difficulty = 5 actually mean?: A five-zero hexadecimal prefix has an expected search cost of 16⁵ attempts, and validation checks integrity, linkage, and work.
sections.Mine a short chain: The example mines blocks at difficulty five and demonstrates the variable time and number of hashes required.
sections.How this relates to Bitcoin:: Bitcoin compares block hashes with a numeric target, adjusts difficulty periodically, and lets nodes verify mined blocks cheaply.
sections.Attack demo: edit data and skip re-minin: Changing block data and recomputing its hash without mining fails the proof-of-work check and disrupts later links.
sections.What proof-of-work actually bought us: Proof-of-work makes producing rewritten history costly while keeping verification inexpensive.
sections.Producing history: Finding a valid block hash may require trying enormous numbers of candidates.
sections.Verifying history: Nodes can verify a block with one hash, while attackers must re-mine rewritten blocks and catch up with honest miners.
sections.Takeaways so far: The article summarizes how hash chaining detects tampering and proof-of-work makes rewriting history computationally expensive.
